answer.label: Not Walt Whitman — an anonymous proverb
answer.authorDates: Earliest print appearance 1862; author never identified
answer.sourceLine: This line does not appear anywhere in Walt Whitman’s published writing. It is a folk saying that circulated anonymously in American newspapers from at least 1862, was misattributed to an obscure “M. B. Whitman” by 1903, and was then mistakenly upgraded to the famous poet “Walt Whitman” by 1919 — almost certainly through confusion over the shared surname, according to Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.

source.excerpt: Face the sunshine, and your shadow will fall behind you.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the saying from an anonymous 1862 newspaper item through a 1903 attribution to an obscure “M. B. Whitman” to its 1919 misattribution to the famous poet: full chronology ↗.

Wikiquote lists the line in Walt Whitman's Misattributed section ↗, stating it “has not been found in either of their published works” (Whitman's or Helen Keller's) and is catalogued as a proverb in A Dictionary of American Proverbs (1992).

A related but distinct variant, “Keep your face to the sunshine and you cannot see the shadows,” is separately credited to Helen Keller by the American Foundation for the Blind ↗, though the Library of Congress noted Keller experts could never locate it in her own writing.

An early poetic cousin appears in Charles Swain's 1850 poem “Youth and Age” (The Literary Gazette, London): “The sun still face to face we meet—/ The shadow falls behind!” — though its exact wording differs from the popular modern saying.
source.excerptNote: The earliest documented close match to the modern quote, printed anonymously—with no author's name attached—in 1862, fifty-seven years before it was ever linked to Walt Whitman.
source.rightsNote: Because this is an untraceable anonymous folk proverb rather than a line from an identified, dated literary work, no reliable public-domain determination can be made for the exact modern wording. The 1862 newspaper item is old enough to be public domain, but its wording (“Face the sunshine, and your shadow will fall behind you”) differs from the popular quote, so the two cannot be treated as the same copyrightable expression.

author.bio: No single author of this saying has ever been identified. Wikiquote ↗ notes it is catalogued as a proverb “commonly used in both the US and Canada” in A Dictionary of American Proverbs (1992). Its imagery echoes an 1850 poem by the minor English poet Charles Swain, but the exact wording was never his either — it appears to have crystallized as an anonymous newspaper adage a decade later.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook case of a floating folk proverb accreting a famous name. The saying predates any Whitman association by decades, and the “Whitman” label itself started out belonging to someone else entirely.

items.why: A Wichita, Kansas newspaper, The Chronicle, printed the saying over the byline “M. B. Whitman” in 1903 — an otherwise unidentified person, per Quote Investigator ↗.

By 1919 the byline had been shortened to just “Whitman” in reprints and was then conflated with the famous poet, per the same Quote Investigator chronology ↗. Wikiquote confirms the line “has not been found” in his published works ↗.

A near-variant, “Keep your face to the sunshine and you cannot see the shadows,” has circulated under Keller's name since 1927 and is still repeated by the American Foundation for the Blind ↗, but the Library of Congress's 1989 Respectfully Quoted reported that Keller specialists could never verify she wrote it.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who first wrote this line — it is an anonymous American adage first seen in print in 1862, and both of its famous namesakes are almost certainly innocent, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Optimism proverbs about sunlight and shadow were everywhere in 19th-century American print culture — short, quotable, moralizing lines that newspapers reprinted freely without bylines. This one likely grew out of that culture rather than from any single author's pen, which is exactly why it was so easy for later editors to slap a famous name on it once its origin had been forgotten.

Once attached to Walt Whitman — already America's most quotable poet of self-reliant optimism — the line spread rapidly through greeting cards, motivational anthologies, and eventually the internet, where it remains one of the most-repeated “Whitman” quotes despite appearing nowhere in Leaves of Grass or his other writings.
